title: In-situ Characterization of High-Temperature Transitions in Materials for Next Generation Computing via STEM Imaging and EELS
content: Above-room temperature electronic transitions in materials are integral to the function of next-generation computing technologies, such as neuromorphic computing, which are poised to make significant improvements in computational speed and energy efficiency. Neuromorphic computing represents a new computing strategy that seeks to emulate the function of neurons and synapses in the brain by controllably and reversibly switching electrical conductivity in devices [1]. In-situ characterization of the nanoscale dynamics that give rise to neuromorphic functionality is crucial for understanding and optimizing these devices and bringing their potential to bear. The combination of high spatial and energy resolution provided by in-situ scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) uniquely positions it to extract insights into these dynamics. However, heating materials in the high vacuum environment of the STEM can lead to unwanted secondary effects, such as sample reduction, that must be controlled before the dynamics of interest can be assessed.
